claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by data showing that knockdown of upd2/3 in EECs increases sleep under normal conditions (Figure 1).

claims.claim: In response to oxidative stress that leads to gut inflammation, elevated Unpaired signaling promotes sleep.
claims.source_text: whereas in response to oxidative stress that leads to gut inflammation, elevated Unpaired signaling instead promotes sleep.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by data showing that animals lacking EEC-derived unpaired fail to increase sleep during oxidative stress (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Stress-induced EEC-derived Upd2/3 activates the JAK–STAT pathway in glial cells at the blood–brain interface.
claims.source_text: Stress-induced EEC-derived Upd2/3 activates the JAK–STAT pathway in glial cells at the blood–brain interface
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter data in glial cells under oxidative stress (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Gut-derived Unpaired signaling influences sleep regulation through glial gating of wake-promoting AstA-mediated signals.
claims.source_text: Our results suggest that gut-derived Unpaired signaling influences sleep regulation through glial gating of wake-promoting AstA-mediated signals
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by data showing AstA receptor downregulation by Unpaired signaling (Figure 7) and inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: upd3 is expressed in EECs under normal homeostatic conditions.
claims.source_text: we observed significant knockdown of the main IL-6 cytokine, upd3 (Oldefest et al., 2013), in dissected adult female midguts (Figure 1A), demonstrating that upd3 is expressed in EECs under normal homeostatic conditions.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data showing upd3 expression in midguts and its knockdown in EECs (Figure 1A).

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd2 or upd3 in EECs increased the amount of time animals spent asleep, especially during the day.
claims.source_text: We found that the knockdown of the two main immune-related cytokines, upd2 or upd3, using voilà> increased the amount of time animals spent asleep (defined as a period of inactivity lasting at least 5 min), especially during the day
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).

claims.claim: EEC-specific loss of upd2 or upd3 promotes sleep with pronounced effects during the daytime.
claims.source_text: This phenotype was reproducible using the more restricted EEC> driver that includes R57C10-GAL80, suggesting that the EEC-specific loss of these cytokines promotes sleep with pronounced effects during the daytime
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data using the EEC-specific driver (Figure 1D–F).

claims.claim: Animals lacking EEC-derived Unpaired signaling exhibited shorter motion bouts.
claims.source_text: Animals lacking EEC-derived Unpaired signaling also exhibited shorter motion bouts (periods of activity; Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by activity monitoring data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J).

claims.claim: EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3 did not reduce motion-bout activity.
claims.source_text: However, the EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3 did not reduce motion-bout activity (the intensity of activity during wake periods), implying that the lack of gut cytokine signaling did not reduce general activity when the animals were awake
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by activity intensity data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K, L).

claims.claim: EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3 did not significantly alter feeding behavior over a 24-hr period.
claims.source_text: We did not detect significant alterations in feeding behavior as a consequence of upd2 or upd3 knockdown in EECs over a 24-hr period using the automated FLIC system
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by FLIC feeding assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).

claims.claim: EEC-specific upd3 overexpression did not affect food consumption.
claims.source_text: nor did we observe an effect of EEC-specific upd3 overexpression on food consumption via a dye assay
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by dye-feeding assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P).

claims.claim: EEC-specific upd3 knockdown did not affect the animals' metabolic state as reflected in their levels of stored triacylglyceride.
claims.source_text: Furthermore, EEC-specific upd3 knockdown did not affect the animals' metabolic state as reflected in their levels of stored triacylglyceride (TAG)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by TAG measurement data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q).

claims.claim: upd3Δ and upd2,3Δ mutants exhibited a pronounced increase in sleep.
claims.source_text: Both mutant lines exhibited a pronounced increase in sleep (Figure 1G–I), with strong effects on daytime sleep, phenocopying the RNAi-mediated knockdown in the EECs.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data in mutant lines (Figure 1G–I).

claims.claim: EEC-specific CRISPR-mediated knockout of upd2 or upd3 led to significantly elevated sleep.
claims.source_text: EEC-specific CRISPR-mediated knockout of upd2 or upd3, induced by UAS-controlled gRNA pairs designed to excise portions of each gene's coding sequence, led to significantly elevated sleep
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from CRISPR knockout experiments (Figure 1J–L).

claims.claim: AstC-positive and Tk-positive EEC populations encompass the vast majority of EECs in the adult Drosophila midgut.
claims.source_text: These two molecularly defined groups encompass the vast majority of EECs.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Guo et al., 2019) and represents established knowledge about EEC populations.

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd2 or upd3 in AstC-positive EECs significantly increased sleep.
claims.source_text: Knockdown of either cytokine in AstC-positive EECs significantly increased sleep (Figure 1M–O), phenocopying the effect observed with knockdown in all EECs
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from AstC-positive EEC-specific knockdown (Figure 1M–O).

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd2 or upd3 in Tk-positive EECs had no significant effect on sleep.
claims.source_text: In contrast, knockdown of upd2 or upd3 in Tk-positive EECs had no significant effect on sleep (Figure 1P–R).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from Tk-positive EEC-specific knockdown (Figure 1P–R).

claims.claim: AstC-positive EECs are a major source of sleep-regulating Unpaired cytokines.
claims.source_text: These findings indicate that AstC-positive EECs are a major source of sleep-regulating Unpaired cytokines
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the differential effects of knockdown in AstC-positive versus Tk-positive EECs.

claims.claim: Tk-positive EECs do not appear to contribute significantly to sleep regulation via Unpaired cytokines.
claims.source_text: whereas Tk-positive EECs do not appear to contribute significantly to this function.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the lack of sleep phenotype when upd2/3 are knocked down in Tk-positive EECs.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal dome knockdown did not significantly alter daytime or nighttime sleep in adult females.
claims.source_text: Pan-neuronal dome knockdown using the driver R57C10-GAL4 (Kubrak et al., 2022) did not significantly alter daytime or nighttime sleep in adult females (Figure 2A)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from neuronal dome knockdown (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Knockdown of dome in glial cells resulted in a pronounced increase in daytime and nighttime sleep.
claims.source_text: In contrast, knockdown of dome in glial cells using the pan-glial driver repo-GAL4 (repo>) resulted in a pronounced increase in daytime and nighttime sleep (Figure 2A)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from glial dome knockdown (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Animals with glial dome knockdown displayed shorter daytime motion bouts.
claims.source_text: Additionally, animals with glial dome knockdown displayed shorter daytime motion bouts, suggesting reduced periods of wakefulness (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by activity monitoring data (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claims.claim: Animals with glial dome knockdown did not exhibit decreased activity during motion bouts.
claims.source_text: without exhibiting decreased activity during these bouts (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by activity intensity data (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claims.claim: Glia-specific dome knockdown did not reduce food intake.
claims.source_text: We also assessed whether glia-specific dome knockdown might affect feeding and energy storage, but we observed no reduction in food intake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by feeding assay data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).

claims.claim: Glia-specific dome knockdown did not change TAG levels.
claims.source_text: and no changes in TAG levels were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by TAG measurement data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd2 or upd3 in EECs led to a marked decrease in JAK–STAT reporter activity within Repo-positive glial cells under normal conditions.
claims.source_text: Knockdown of either upd2 or upd3 in the EECs led to a marked decrease in JAK–STAT reporter activity within Repo-positive glial cells under normal conditions (Figure 2G, H)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter imaging data (Figure 2G, H).

claims.claim: Upd2/3-mediated signaling from the EECs to the brain's glial cells activates JAK–STAT signaling.
claims.source_text: suggesting that Upd2/3-mediated signaling from the EECs to the brain's glial cells activates JAK–STAT signaling.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the decrease in glial JAK-STAT activity when EEC upd2/3 are knocked down.

claims.claim: Gut-to-glia communication via Upd2 and Upd3 modulates diurnal sleep patterns through glial JAK–STAT activation.
claims.source_text: Taken together, this suggests that gut-to-glia communication via Upd2 and Upd3 modulates diurnal sleep patterns through glial JAK–STAT activation
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined data showing effects of EEC upd2/3 and glial dome on sleep and JAK-STAT activity.

claims.claim: Upd2 and Upd3 are required for the maintenance of wakefulness during the day under healthy conditions.
claims.source_text: and that these cytokines are required for the maintenance of wakefulness during the day under healthy conditions.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the increased sleep observed when these cytokines are knocked down under normal conditions.

claims.claim: Gut infection leads to increased ROS levels and induces local cytokine production.
claims.source_text: Gut infection leads to increased ROS levels and induces local cytokine production
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations (Jiang et al., 2009; Buchon et al., 2013; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007) and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Oxidative stress is a key feature of inflammatory conditions in the intestine.
claims.source_text: and oxidative stress is a key feature of inflammatory conditions in the intestine
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Aviello and Knaus, 2017) and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Dietary H2O2 treatment leads to local intestinal responses comparable to those observed during pathogenic challenges.
claims.source_text: Dietary H2O2 treatment leads to local intestinal responses comparable to those observed during pathogenic challenges
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citation (Tamamouna et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Feeding with 1% H2O2 substantially upregulated upd3 expression in dissected midguts of females.
claims.source_text: we found substantial upregulation of upd3 expression in dissected midguts of females challenged with ROS by feeding 1% H2O2 in adult-specific, cornmeal-free diet for 20 hr (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data showing upd3 upregulation after H2O2 treatment (Figure 3A).

claims.claim: Oxidative stress promoted upd2 expression, albeit to a lesser extent than upd3.
claims.source_text: Oxidative stress also promoted upd2 expression, albeit to a lesser extent
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data (Figure 3A).

claims.claim: Exposure to 0.1% H2O2 incrementally increased daytime sleep amount over successive days.
claims.source_text: Exposure to a lower H2O2 concentration (0.1%) incrementally increased daytime sleep amount over successive days (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: Exposure to 1% H2O2 triggered an immediate augmentation of daytime sleep.
claims.source_text: In contrast, a higher H2O2 concentration (1%) triggered an immediate augmentation of daytime sleep (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data (Figure 3C).

claims.claim: Intestinal oxidative stress dose-dependently modulates sleep.
claims.source_text: These observations suggest that intestinal oxidative stress dose-dependently modulates sleep.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the differential effects of 0.1% versus 1% H2O2 on sleep.

claims.claim: EEC-specific RNAi targeting upd2 or upd3 abolished the sleep response to 1%-H2O2 feeding.
claims.source_text: Indeed, EEC-specific RNAi targeting upd2 or upd3 abolished the sleep response to 1%-H2O2 feeding.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data showing no increase in sleep during H2O2 treatment when upd2/3 are knocked down in EECs (Figure 3D, E).

claims.claim: Animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3 did not exhibit increased daytime sleep in response to intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: Animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3 did not exhibit increased daytime sleep in response to the induction of oxidative stress in the intestine, even over two consecutive days of exposure to 1% H2O2-containing diet
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data (Figure 3D, E).

claims.claim: Animals lacking upd3 in the EECs appeared to lose nighttime sleep in response to enteric stress.
claims.source_text: Intriguingly, animals lacking upd3 in the EECs not only did not increase their sleep under oxidative stress but indeed appeared to lose nighttime sleep in response to enteric stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 3D, E).

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd2 or upd3 limited to the AstC-positive EEC subpopulation prevented the H2O2-induced increase in sleep.
claims.source_text: Moreover, knockdown of upd2 or upd3 limited to the AstC-positive EEC subpopulation still prevented the H2O2-induced increase in sleep (Figure 3F–H).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from AstC-positive EEC-specific knockdown under oxidative stress (Figure 3F–H).

claims.claim: Unpaired signaling from AstC-positive EECs is necessary for mediating the sleep response to intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: These findings indicate that Unpaired signaling from AstC-positive EECs is necessary for mediating the sleep response to intestinal oxidative stress
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the loss of ROS-induced sleep response when upd2/3 are knocked down in AstC-positive EECs.

claims.claim: Animals with upd2 or upd3 knockdown in EECs displayed no additional sensitivity to oxidative stress in survival assays.
claims.source_text: However, when we assessed survival on 1% H2O2-containing food, animals with upd2 or upd3 knockdown in EECs displayed no additional sensitivity to oxidative stress, compared to controls (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by survival assay data (Figure 3I).

claims.claim: 1%-H2O2 feeding for 24 hr does not cause increased neuronal cell death.
claims.source_text: Using a TUNEL assay for apoptosis, we found no evidence of increased neuronal cell death in animals fed 1% H2O2 for 24 hr
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by TUNEL staining data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).

claims.claim: Animals lacking EEC-derived upd3 suppressed their sleep to a similar extent as controls in response to starvation.
claims.source_text: Animals lacking EEC-derived upd3 suppressed their sleep to a similar extent as controls in response to starvation, indicating a normal sleep response to nutritional stress
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data during starvation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).

claims.claim: upd3Δ and upd2,3Δ mutants showed a strong reduction in daytime and nighttime sleep under oxidative-stress conditions.
claims.source_text: Whereas upd3Δ and upd2,3Δ mutants exhibited increased baseline sleep under homeostatic conditions, these animals not only failed to increase their sleep in response to oxidative stress but indeed showed a strong reduction in daytime and nighttime sleep under oxidative-stress conditions (Figure 3J–L).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data in mutants under oxidative stress (Figure 3J–L).

claims.claim: Low Unpaired signaling promotes wakefulness under normal conditions, whereas higher ROS-induced Unpaired signaling facilitates a shift to restorative sleep during intestinal stress.
claims.source_text: This indicates a dual functionality of Unpaired cytokine signaling, in which low Unpaired signaling promotes wakefulness under normal conditions, whereas higher ROS-induced Unpaired signaling facilitates a shift to restorative sleep during intestinal stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined data showing opposite effects of upd2/3 loss under normal versus stress conditions.

claims.claim: Animals overexpressing upd3 in the EECs exhibited increased sleep during the day, even in the absence of H2O2-induced oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: Consistent with a model in which high levels of Upd3, like those that would occur during periods of elevated intestinal oxidative stress, promote daytime sleep, animals overexpressing upd3 in the EECs exhibited increased sleep during the day, even in the absence of H2O2-induced oxidative stress (Figure 3M, N).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from upd3 overexpression experiments (Figure 3M, N).

claims.claim: Animals with EEC-specific upd3 overexpression further increased their sleep in response to H2O2-induced enteric oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: These animals further increased their sleep in response to H2O2-induced enteric oxidative stress, unlike those lacking gut-derived upd3 (Figure 3D, E)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 3M, N).

claims.claim: After animals were switched back to normal food after one day of oxidative stress, both control animals and those with EEC-specific upd3 overexpression exhibited even more sleep than during the previous day under oxidative-stress conditions.
claims.source_text: After the animals were switched back to normal food after one day of oxidative stress, both control animals and those with EEC-specific upd3 overexpression exhibited even more sleep than during the previous day under oxidative-stress conditions (Figure 3M, N).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data during recovery (Figure 3M, N).

claims.claim: Glial JAK–STAT reporter activity was upregulated by oxidative stress at ZT0 in animals fed for 20 hr with 1% H2O2-containing food.
claims.source_text: However, we observed a significant increase in GFP signal at ZT0 in animals fed for 20 hr with 1% H2O2-containing food, indicating recent JAK–STAT activity in the surface glia.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter imaging data (Figure 4A, B).

claims.claim: Glial JAK–STAT reporter activity upregulation by oxidative stress was abolished in animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3.
claims.source_text: Whereas glial JAK–STAT reporter activity was upregulated by oxidative stress (20 hrs' 1%-H2O2 feeding) in control animals, this response was abolished in animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd2 or upd3, indicating that this response is dependent on these EEC-derived cytokines (Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter data (Figure 4C, D).

claims.claim: dome transcript levels in heads were upregulated in animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd3 exposed to oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: We observed an upregulation of dome transcript levels in the heads of animals with EEC-specific knockdown of upd3, exposed to oxidative stress induced by 15 hr of feeding with food laced with 1% H2O2 (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: Increased dome expression suggests reduced Unpaired ligand availability as a result of the loss of EEC-derived Upd3.
claims.source_text: Increased dome expression suggests reduced Unpaired ligand availability as a result of the loss of EEC-derived Upd3.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the compensatory upregulation of receptor expression in response to reduced ligand.

claims.claim: EEC-derived Unpaired cytokine signaling is required for activating glial JAK–STAT under oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: Together, our results demonstrate that EEC-derived Unpaired cytokine signaling is required for activating glial JAK–STAT under oxidative stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined data showing loss of glial JAK-STAT activation when EEC upd2/3 are knocked down.

claims.claim: Knockdown of dome in all glial cells completely abolished the ROS-induced daytime-sleep response when animals were fed a 1%-H2O2 supplemented diet.
claims.source_text: Knockdown of dome in all glial cells using the repo> driver completely abolished the ROS-induced daytime-sleep response when animals were fed a 1%-H2O2 supplemented diet.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).

claims.claim: Glia-specific dome knockdown resulted in progressive and substantial sleep loss over two consecutive days on 1% H2O2-containing food.
claims.source_text: Mirroring the effects observed with upd2,3Δ mutants (Figure 3G–I), glia-specific dome knockdown (p < 0.00001 for dome-iKK and p = 0.0556 for dome-iTRiP) resulted in progressive and substantial sleep loss over two consecutive days on 1% H2O2-containing food.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep monitoring data (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: In response to 1% H2O2-containing food, animals lacking glial dome expression displayed a reduction in sleep duration rather than an increase.
claims.source_text: The results showed that, in response to 1% H2O2-containing food, animals lacking glial dome expression displayed a sleep response opposite from that of controls, with a reduction in sleep duration rather than an increase
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: During the recovery phase after oxidative stress, the sleep level of controls increased even further, but the sleep duration exhibited by animals with glia-specific dome knockdown immediately reverted to pre-stress levels.
claims.source_text: During the recovery phase, after the animals had been switched back to normal food, the sleep level of controls increased even further, but the sleep duration exhibited by animals with glia-specific dome knockdown immediately reverted to pre-stress levels.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data during recovery (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: dome knockdown in glial cells did not decrease survival on H2O2-containing food.
claims.source_text: In line with this and paralleling the loss of upd2 or upd3 in the EECs, dome knockdown in glial cells did not decrease survival on H2O2-containing food (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by survival assay data (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Animals with glial-specific dome knockdown exhibited increased sleep (rebound sleep) in the morning hours following sleep deprivation.
claims.source_text: Like controls, animals with glial-specific dome knockdown exhibited increased sleep (rebound sleep) in the morning hours (ZT0–ZT2) following sleep deprivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep rebound data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).

claims.claim: Dome-mediated JAK–STAT signaling in glial cells specifically regulates ROS-induced sleep responses.
claims.source_text: Collectively, these data suggest that Dome-mediated JAK–STAT signaling in the glial cells specifically regulates ROS-induced sleep responses.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the specific loss of ROS-induced sleep response but normal rebound sleep in glial dome knockdown animals.

claims.claim: In animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown or glia-specific dome RNAi, exposure to 4% H2O2-containing food led to a pronounced loss of sleep during the daytime.
claims.source_text: However, in animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown or glia-specific dome RNAi, exposure to 4% H2O2-containing food led to a pronounced loss of sleep during the daytime.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data under high oxidative stress (Figure 5E–I).

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd3 in the EECs resulted in decreased GFP intensity in the outermost glial cell layer of the central brain after 15 hr of exposure to 1% H2O2-containing food.
claims.source_text: Knockdown of upd3 in the EECs using voilà> (without R57C10-GAL80), which in this assay drives specific knockdown in the gut without detectable neuronal effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B), resulted in decreased GFP intensity in the outermost glial cell layer of the central brain facing the periphery after 15 hr of exposure to 1% H2O2-containing food, indicating reduced JAK–STAT activity in these cells (Figure 6A, B).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter imaging data in BBB glia (Figure 6A, B).

claims.claim: EEC-specific upd3 knockdown did not affect JAK–STAT activity in the outer glial layer of the ventral nerve cord.
claims.source_text: Interestingly, this knockdown did not affect JAK–STAT activity in the outer glial layer of the ventral nerve cord (VNC), suggesting that Upd3 acts specifically on brain BBB glia in response to intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by JAK-STAT reporter imaging data (Figure 6A, B).

claims.claim: Knockdown of dome in BBB glial cells led to increased sleep during normal homeostatic conditions.
claims.source_text: As observed with other manipulations, knockdown of dome in these BBB glial cells led to increased sleep during normal homeostatic conditions (Figure 6C–F).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from BBB-specific dome knockdown (Figure 6C–F).

claims.claim: Loss of dome in the subperineurial BBB glia blocked the ROS-induced sleep increase during 1%-H2O2 exposure and recovery.
claims.source_text: Control animals exhibited the expected sleep increase both during 1%-H2O2 exposure and during the recovery period, but loss of dome in the subperineurial BBB glia blocked these effects (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 6C, D).

claims.claim: dome-RNAi in BBB glial cells led to sleep loss in response to 4% H2O2-containing food.
claims.source_text: When oxidative stress levels were elevated further using 4% H2O2-containing food, dome-RNAi in BBB glial cells led to sleep loss in response to oxidative stress, with sleep levels rebounding to pre-stress levels on the subsequent recovery day when animals were returned to a normal diet (Figure 6E, F).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data under high oxidative stress (Figure 6E, F).

claims.claim: Dome-mediated JAK–STAT activation in the subperineurial BBB cells is required for maintaining an increased sleep state during intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: These results indicate that disrupting dome specifically in the subperineurial glial cells of the BBB recapitulates the phenotypes observed with pan-glial dome knockdown or with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown, and they suggest that Dome-mediated JAK–STAT activation in the subperineurial BBB cells is required for maintaining an increased sleep state during intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the phenocopy of pan-glial and EEC-specific manipulations by BBB-specific dome knockdown.

claims.claim: Expressing hyperactivated JAK (HopTum) in BBB glia led to increased sleep under normal conditions.
claims.source_text: Expressing this protein in BBB glia led to increased sleep under normal conditions (without unusual oxidative stress), consistent with a sleep-promoting effect of high JAK–STAT signaling (Figure 6C–F).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from HopTum overexpression (Figure 6C–F).

claims.claim: Animals with overactive JAK signaling in BBB glia exhibited a further increase in sleep both during oxidative stress and in the subsequent recovery phase.
claims.source_text: Moreover, animals with overactive JAK signaling in BBB glia exhibited a further increase in sleep both during oxidative stress and in the subsequent recovery phase, in contrast to the effects seen with dome knockdown.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data from HopTum overexpression under oxidative stress (Figure 6C–F).

claims.claim: JAK–STAT signaling specifically in the subperineurial glial of the BBB links sleep responses to intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: Collectively, our data indicate that JAK–STAT signaling specifically in the subperineurial glial of the BBB links sleep responses to intestinal oxidative stress.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined data showing BBB-specific effects on sleep regulation during oxidative stress.

claims.claim: AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 ranked among the top 4% of genes most strongly downregulated by JAK/STAT signaling in glia following enteric infection.
claims.source_text: The receptors for Allatostatin A (AstA), AstA-R1 and AstA-R2, both ranked among the top 4% of genes most strongly downregulated by JAK/STAT signaling (with AstA-R1 expression reduced by ~80% and AstA-R2 by ~90%).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is based on published dataset analysis (Cai et al., 2021).

claims.claim: AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 were the only peptide-hormone G-protein-coupled receptors downregulated in JAK–STAT-activated glial cells.
claims.source_text: Notably, these were the only peptide-hormone G-protein-coupled receptors downregulated in the JAK–STAT-activated glial cells.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is based on analysis of published data (Cai et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The outer layer of glial cells at the BBB expresses both AstA-R1 and AstA-R2.
claims.source_text: We observed that the outer layer of glial cells at the barrier between the brain and the periphery – constituting the BBB – expresses both AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Knockdown of AstA-R2 in BBB glia led to a significant reduction in AstA-R2 transcript levels in dissected brains.
claims.source_text: This led to a significant reduction in AstA-R2 transcript levels in dissected brains, indicating that BBB glia are a significant source of AstA-R2 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 expression was upregulated in the heads of animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown following gut-oxidative stress.
claims.source_text: In support of an inhibitory role of Unpaired signaling, we observed that AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 expression was upregulated in the heads of animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown, following gut-oxidative stress induced by feeding with 1% H2O2-laced food for 20 hr (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data (Figure 7B).

claims.claim: Glial-specific dome knockdown led to strong upregulation of both AstA-R1 and AstA-R2 in animals fed 1% H2O2-containing food for 20 hr.
claims.source_text: Indeed, glial-specific dome knockdown led to strong upregulation of both AstA-R1 and AstA-R2, indicating that ROS-induced glia-mediated Unpaired signaling is inhibiting AstA receptor expression (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qPCR data (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: Knocking down AstA-R1 or AstA-R2 in BBB glia attenuated the ROS-induced sleep response.
claims.source_text: Consistent with this notion, we found that knocking down AstA-R1 or AstA-R2 in BBB glia attenuated the ROS-induced sleep response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sleep data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).

results.result: Gut-derived Unpaired cytokine signaling from enteroendocrine cells (EECs) to brain glial cells exhibits dual functionality in sleep regulation: under normal conditions, it promotes wakefulness, while elevated signaling during oxidative stress induces sleep. This dose-dependent effect represents a context-specific modulation of sleep behavior.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C2-C4, C52-C54, and C99 collectively demonstrate this dual functionality through multiple lines of evidence: RNAi knockdown experiments showing increased sleep under normal conditions (C3, C53, C58-C59), loss of stress-induced sleep response when cytokines are knocked down (C4, C54, C90-C91), and mutant analysis confirming opposite effects under normal versus stress conditions (C65, C98). The dose-dependent model (C99) is well-supported by the contrasting phenotypes observed across different experimental conditions.

results.result: Unpaired cytokines upd2 and upd3 are expressed in enteroendocrine cells under normal conditions, with AstC-positive EECs identified as the major source of sleep-regulating Unpaired cytokines. Loss of these cytokines in EECs increases sleep, particularly during daytime.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C57-C71 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: qPCR demonstrating upd3 expression in EECs (C57), RNAi knockdown showing increased sleep (C58-C59), genetic mutants phenocopying RNAi effects (C65), CRISPR-mediated knockout confirming the phenotype (C66), and cell-type-specific manipulations identifying AstC-positive EECs as the critical source (C68-C71). The consistency across independent methods and multiple RNAi lines strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Glial cells, but not neurons, are the CNS targets of gut-derived Unpaired signaling. Knockdown of the Unpaired receptor dome in glia increases sleep and reduces JAK-STAT reporter activity, demonstrating that gut-to-glia communication via Upd2/3 modulates sleep through glial JAK-STAT activation.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C72-C81 establish glia as the critical CNS target through complementary experiments: neuronal dome knockdown shows no sleep phenotype (C72), while glial knockdown phenocopies EEC cytokine loss (C73). The functional connection is demonstrated by JAK-STAT reporter experiments showing reduced glial activity when EEC cytokines are knocked down (C78-C79). Multiple independent RNAi lines confirm the glial phenotype (C73), ruling out off-target effects.

results.result: Intestinal oxidative stress induced by H2O2 feeding upregulates upd2 and upd3 expression in the gut and dose-dependently modulates sleep, with higher concentrations (1% H2O2) triggering immediate sleep increases and lower concentrations (0.1% H2O2) causing gradual sleep augmentation.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C5 and C85-C89 demonstrate oxidative stress effects through qPCR showing cytokine upregulation (C5, C85-C86) and behavioral assays revealing dose-dependent sleep responses (C87-C89). The dose-response relationship is clearly established with two different H2O2 concentrations producing distinct temporal patterns of sleep increase. Control experiments rule out procedural artifacts.

results.result: EEC-derived Unpaired signaling from AstC-positive EECs is necessary for the sleep response to intestinal oxidative stress. Animals lacking upd2/3 in EECs fail to increase sleep during oxidative stress and instead show sleep loss, particularly at night.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C90-C94 and C98 demonstrate the requirement for EEC-derived cytokines in stress-induced sleep through loss-of-function experiments: RNAi knockdown abolishes the H2O2-induced sleep increase (C90-C91), with some animals showing paradoxical sleep loss (C92). Cell-type-specific knockdown in AstC-positive EECs recapitulates this phenotype (C93-C94), and genetic mutants show even stronger effects (C98). Multiple independent RNAi lines confirm specificity.

results.result: Oxidative stress-induced Unpaired cytokines from EECs activate JAK-STAT signaling in glial cells. This activation is abolished when upd2 or upd3 are knocked down in EECs, demonstrating that EEC-derived cytokines are required for glial JAK-STAT activation under oxidative stress.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C6, C55, C103-C104, and C107 establish the functional connection between gut cytokines and glial JAK-STAT activation through reporter assays. The temporal reporter system shows increased glial JAK-STAT activity during oxidative stress (C103), and this response is lost when EEC cytokines are knocked down (C104). Compensatory upregulation of the dome receptor when ligand is reduced (C105-C106) provides additional support for the signaling relationship.

results.result: Glial JAK-STAT signaling is required for maintaining elevated sleep during oxidative stress-induced intestinal disturbances. Knockdown of dome in glia abolishes the ROS-induced sleep increase and causes sleep loss during oxidative stress, with immediate reversion to baseline during recovery.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C7-C111, C114, and C119 demonstrate the requirement for glial JAK-STAT in stress-induced sleep through multiple experiments: pan-glial dome knockdown abolishes ROS-induced sleep increase (C108), causes progressive sleep loss during stress (C109-C110), and shows abnormal recovery dynamics (C111). The specificity is confirmed by normal rebound sleep after deprivation (C113), indicating selective impairment of ROS-induced responses. Multiple RNAi lines and adult-restricted knockdown confirm the phenotype.

results.result: JAK-STAT signaling specifically in subperineurial glial cells of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is both necessary and sufficient for sleep responses to intestinal oxidative stress. BBB-specific dome knockdown phenocopies pan-glial effects, while hyperactivation of JAK in BBB glia increases sleep.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C116-C124 identify BBB glia as the critical glial subtype through anatomical and functional experiments: JAK-STAT reporter activity in BBB glia is reduced when EEC upd3 is knocked down (C116), BBB-specific dome knockdown recapitulates pan-glial phenotypes (C118-C121), and hyperactivated JAK in BBB glia increases sleep (C122-C123). The brain-specific effect (no VNC involvement, C117) further supports the anatomical specificity of this pathway.

results.result: Gut-derived Allatostatin A (AstA) from enteroendocrine cells acts as a wake-promoting signal. Knockdown of AstA in AstA-positive EECs increases sleep, and activation of these EECs suppresses sleep in an AstA-dependent manner.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C8, C135, and C136 establish AstA as a wake-promoting factor through complementary loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments: RNAi knockdown of AstA in EECs increases sleep with two independent RNAi lines (C135), and TrpA1-mediated activation of AstA-positive EECs suppresses sleep, an effect abolished by simultaneous AstA knockdown (C136). The gut-specific driver ensures the phenotype is due to gut-derived AstA.

results.result: During intestinal oxidative stress, gut-derived Unpaired cytokines inhibit AstA receptor expression in BBB glia through JAK-STAT activation. AstA receptors (AstA-R1 and AstA-R2) are expressed in BBB glia, downregulated by JAK-STAT signaling, and required for the ROS-induced sleep response.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C9, C56, C125-C133 establish the mechanism by which Unpaired signaling gates AstA signaling through multiple lines of evidence: published data showing AstA receptors are downregulated by JAK-STAT (C125-C126), immunohistochemistry confirming BBB glial expression (C127), qPCR showing upregulation when Unpaired signaling is blocked (C129-C130), and functional experiments demonstrating that AstA receptor knockdown in BBB glia attenuates ROS-induced sleep responses (C131-C132) while increasing baseline sleep (C133). The convergence of anatomical, molecular, and functional data strongly supports this gating mechanism.

results.result: Oxidative stress suppresses AstA expression and release from EECs, as evidenced by reduced transcript levels and peptide accumulation. This dual-site regulation—suppression at the source (gut) and target (BBB glia via Unpaired signaling)—silences wake-promoting AstA signaling during intestinal stress.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C137-C140 demonstrate coordinated suppression of AstA signaling through qPCR showing reduced transcript levels (C137), immunostaining showing peptide accumulation suggesting reduced release (C137-C138), and single-cell RNA-seq data showing AstA-positive EECs lack TrpA1 (C139), consistent with lack of ROS-induced release. The model of dual-site regulation (C140) integrates these observations with the receptor downregulation data. However, the mechanism of AstA suppression at the source remains incompletely defined.

results.result: Overexpression of upd3 in EECs increases sleep even under normal conditions and further enhances sleep during oxidative stress, with elevated recovery sleep following stress removal. This demonstrates that high levels of Upd3 are sufficient to promote sleep.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C100-C102 establish sufficiency of elevated Upd3 for sleep promotion through gain-of-function experiments: EEC-specific upd3 overexpression increases baseline sleep (C100), further increases sleep during H2O2 exposure (C101), and enhances recovery sleep (C102). The overexpression drives upd3 to levels comparable to those induced by oxidative stress, supporting the physiological relevance of the manipulation.

results.result: Animals lacking EEC-derived Unpaired signaling or glial dome exhibit shorter motion bouts (reduced wakefulness periods) without decreased activity intensity during wake periods, indicating specific effects on sleep regulation rather than general activity impairment.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C60-C61 and C74-C75 demonstrate that the sleep phenotypes are not due to general activity deficits through detailed behavioral analysis: both EEC cytokine knockdown and glial dome knockdown reduce motion bout duration (C60, C74) but do not reduce activity intensity during wake periods (C61, C75). This dissociation indicates specific regulation of sleep/wake transitions rather than motor impairment or general sickness.

results.result: Manipulations of EEC-derived Unpaired signaling or glial dome do not significantly affect feeding behavior or metabolic state (TAG levels), indicating that the observed sleep phenotypes are independent of changes in feeding or energy metabolism.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C62-C64 and C76-C77 rule out metabolic and feeding confounds through multiple assays: FLIC automated feeding monitoring shows no change in feeding behavior with EEC cytokine knockdown (C62), dye-feeding assays show no effect of upd3 overexpression (C63), and TAG measurements show no metabolic changes with either EEC cytokine knockdown (C64) or glial dome knockdown (C77). These controls strengthen the conclusion that the pathway specifically regulates sleep.

results.result: Loss of EEC-derived Unpaired signaling or glial dome does not increase sensitivity to oxidative stress (survival), cause neuronal cell death, or impair starvation-induced sleep suppression or sleep deprivation-induced rebound sleep, indicating specific impairment of ROS-induced sleep responses.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C95-C97, C112-C113 demonstrate the specificity of the pathway through multiple control experiments: survival assays show no increased oxidative stress sensitivity (C95, C112), TUNEL staining shows no neuronal apoptosis (C96), starvation responses remain normal (C97), and sleep deprivation-induced rebound sleep is intact (C113). These controls rule out general physiological impairment and indicate selective disruption of the ROS-induced sleep pathway.

results.result: Dome receptor transcript levels are upregulated in heads of animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown during oxidative stress, suggesting compensatory upregulation in response to reduced ligand availability.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C105-C106 demonstrate compensatory receptor upregulation through qPCR showing increased dome expression when EEC upd3 is knocked down during oxidative stress (C105). This pattern is consistent with homeostatic receptor regulation in response to reduced ligand (C106) and provides additional evidence that gut-derived Upd3 normally signals to the brain. However, the interpretation as compensatory regulation, while reasonable, is inferential.

results.result: Under high oxidative stress (4% H2O2), animals with EEC-specific upd3 knockdown or glia-specific dome knockdown show pronounced daytime sleep loss, demonstrating that the pathway is required across different stress intensities.
results.result_reasoning: Claim C115 extends the findings to higher stress levels, showing that both EEC cytokine knockdown and glial dome knockdown cause sleep loss under 4% H2O2 conditions. This demonstrates that the pathway requirement is not limited to a narrow range of stress intensity and suggests dose-dependent effects across a broad range of oxidative stress levels.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that Unpaired cytokines (upd2 and upd3) from enteroendocrine cells (EECs) regulate sleep in a dual manner: under normal conditions, EEC-derived Unpaired signaling promotes wakefulness, while elevated Unpaired signaling in response to oxidative stress induces sleep. This was shown through RNAi knockdown, mutant analysis, and CRISPR-mediated knockout experiments, with specific effects traced to AstC-positive EEC subpopulations.
results.result_reasoning: The first reviewer states the work is 'supported by well-designed and well-performed experiments, especially those that show that the endocrine cells from the gut are the sources of the Upd cytokines, the effects of these cytokines on daytime sleep.' The editor notes 'The evidence is compelling and elegantly performed.' No concerns were raised about these core findings regarding EEC-derived cytokines and their dual role in sleep regulation.

results.result: The authors show that Unpaired cytokines activate JAK-STAT signaling in glial cells, particularly those of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and that this glial JAK-STAT activation is required for maintaining elevated sleep during oxidative stress-induced intestinal disturbances. BBB-specific dome knockdown phenocopied pan-glial and EEC-specific manipulations, demonstrating that subperineurial BBB glia are the critical target cells.
results.result_reasoning: The first reviewer explicitly states 'the evidence is compelling' for experiments 'that show...the glial cells of the BBB are the target cell for the Upds action.' The editor confirms 'cytokines Upd3 and Upd2 produced by the intestine following inflammation act on glia of the blood brain barrier to regulate sleep.' No methodological concerns were raised about the glial targeting experiments.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that Allatostatin A (AstA) from EECs promotes wakefulness, and that during oxidative stress, gut-derived Unpaired cytokines inhibit AstA receptor expression in BBB glia through JAK-STAT signaling, thereby blocking wake-promoting signals. This was supported by receptor expression analysis, knockdown experiments, and EEC activation studies showing AstA's wake-promoting role.
results.result_reasoning: The first reviewer states 'the evidence associating the downregulation of Alst receptors in the BBB by Upd and Jak/Stat pathways is compelling.' The editor summarizes the findings as showing the mechanism 'by modulating Allatostatin A signaling.' No concerns were raised about the AstA receptor experiments or the proposed mechanism of glial gating.

results.result: The authors used dietary H2O2 treatment to induce oxidative stress as a model of gut inflammation, showing that this treatment upregulates upd2 and upd3 expression in EECs and dose-dependently increases sleep. Animals lacking EEC-derived Unpaired cytokines failed to increase sleep in response to H2O2-induced oxidative stress.
results.result_reasoning: The reviewer raises significant concerns about the oxidative stress model, stating 'The model of gut inflammation that is used is based on the increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) that is caused by adding 1% H2O2 to the food. The use of the model is supported rather weakly by two papers' and 'There is no support for the use of ROS in the food instead a direct infection by pathogenic bacteria. It is known that ROS causes damage in the gut epithelium, which in turn induces the expression of the cytokines studied, which might be independent of infection and confound the results.' This critique questions whether the H2O2 model appropriately represents infection-induced inflammation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations agree that EEC-derived cytokines have a dual role in sleep regulation. OpenEval R1 covers claims C2-C4, C52-C54, C99 focusing on the dual functionality under normal vs stress conditions. Peer R1 covers a broader set including C2-C4, C52-C59, C65-C71 and confirms the evidence is 'compelling and elegantly performed' for EEC sources of Upd cytokines and their effects on daytime sleep.

Both evaluations support the identification of EEC-derived cytokines through multiple experimental approaches. OpenEval R2 focuses specifically on claims C57-C71 demonstrating upd3 expression and function in EECs using qPCR, RNAi, CRISPR, and cell-type-specific manipulations. Peer R1 includes these claims and states the evidence is 'well-designed and well-performed' for showing endocrine cells as sources of Upd cytokines.

Both evaluations agree on glia as the critical CNS target. OpenEval R3 covers claims C72-C73, C78-C81 establishing glia through neuronal vs glial knockdown experiments and JAK-STAT reporter assays. Peer R2 includes C73, C78-C81 among others and states 'the evidence is compelling' for showing 'glial cells of the BBB are the target cell for the Upds action.'

Both evaluations support the functional connection between gut cytokines and glial JAK-STAT activation. OpenEval R6 covers claims C6, C55, C103-C104, C107 using reporter assays showing increased glial JAK-STAT activity during stress. Peer R2 includes C6, C103-C104, C107 and confirms cytokines act on BBB glia to regulate sleep.

Both evaluations support the requirement for glial JAK-STAT in stress-induced sleep. OpenEval R7 covers claims C7-C111, C114, C119 showing pan-glial dome knockdown abolishes ROS-induced sleep. Peer R2 includes C7, C108-C111, C114, C119 and confirms the evidence for BBB glia as targets is compelling.

Both evaluations support BBB glia as the critical glial subtype. OpenEval R8 covers claims C116-C124 identifying BBB glia through anatomical and functional experiments including JAK-STAT reporter activity and BBB-specific dome knockdown. Peer R2 includes all these claims (C116-C124) and explicitly states evidence is compelling for 'glial cells of the BBB' as the target.

Both evaluations support AstA as a wake-promoting factor. OpenEval R9 covers claims C8, C135-C136 showing RNAi knockdown increases sleep and TrpA1 activation suppresses sleep. Peer R3 includes C8, C135-C136 and states evidence is compelling for the role of AstA in the mechanism.

Both evaluations strongly support the mechanism by which Unpaired signaling gates AstA signaling. OpenEval R10 covers claims C9, C56, C125-C133 showing AstA receptors are downregulated by JAK-STAT through multiple lines of evidence. Peer R3 includes C9, C125-C127, C129-C133 and explicitly states 'the evidence associating the downregulation of Alst receptors in the BBB by Upd and Jak/Stat pathways is compelling.'

Both evaluations support coordinated suppression of AstA signaling. OpenEval R11 covers claims C137-C140 showing reduced transcript levels, peptide accumulation, and dual-site regulation. Peer R3 includes C137-C138, C140 and confirms the evidence for AstA modulation is compelling, though OpenEval notes the mechanism at the source remains incompletely defined.

Disagreement on oxidative stress model validity. OpenEval R4 finds claims C5, C85-C89 demonstrating oxidative stress effects through qPCR and dose-dependent sleep responses are SUPPORTED. Peer R4 rates these claims UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that 'The model of gut inflammation...is supported rather weakly' and that 'ROS causes damage in the gut epithelium...which might be independent of infection and confound the results.'

Disagreement on stress-induced sleep requirement for EEC cytokines. OpenEval R5 finds claims C90-C94, C98 showing RNAi knockdown abolishes H2O2-induced sleep are SUPPORTED. Peer R4 includes C90-C91, C93-C94, C98 but rates them UNCERTAIN due to concerns about whether the H2O2 model appropriately represents infection-induced inflammation rather than non-specific epithelial damage.

Disagreement on sufficiency of elevated Upd3. OpenEval R12 finds claims C100-C102 showing EEC-specific upd3 overexpression increases sleep are SUPPORTED. Peer R4 includes C100-C101 but rates them UNCERTAIN, likely due to the broader concern about the H2O2 model's validity as a representation of infection-induced inflammation.

Disagreement on higher stress level effects. OpenEval R17 finds claim C115 showing sleep loss under 4% H2O2 is SUPPORTED. Peer R4 includes C115 but rates it UNCERTAIN due to concerns about the H2O2 model not appropriately representing pathogenic infection and potentially causing confounding epithelial damage.
